opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons. The first is that in systems, the real test of an idea is whether it works in practice. You can write a paper, you can show some nice benchmarks, but the moment real people start using what you've built, you learn things you would never have discovered otherwise. Users push the system in directions you didn't anticipate, they hit corner cases, they have workloads that look nothing like the ones you designed for. And that feedback loop is incredibly valuable, because it tells you which problems actually matter and which ones you just imagined.

The second reason is impact. As academics, we want our work to make a difference, and in systems, one of the most direct ways to have impact is for people to actually adopt what you build. If you look at projects that came out of Berkeley over the years, from BSD and Postgres to Spark and Ray, much of their influence came from the fact that they were real, usable systems, not just ideas on paper. People could pick them up and build on them.

And third, building real systems is a great way to train students. When you build something people depend on, you have to think about everything: performance, reliability, usability, APIs, documentation. Students learn to make tradeoffs and to understand the whole stack, and they also learn to listen to users. That's a skill that serves them well whether they go into academia, start a company, or join industry.

There's also a nice side effect: once you have users, you have a source of new research problems. The system becomes a kind of laboratory. Each time people run into a limitation, that's potentially the next research project. So it's not a distraction from research; it's actually one of the best engines for generating good research.

r001.rationale: The candidate says users expose unexpected limitations that can become research projects, but does not explain that building a system in a new area gives researchers a privileged position to discover that area's emerging problems.

r002.rationale: The candidate says user feedback reveals which problems matter, but does not connect problems left unsolved by industry with a lack of importance at the present time.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there are a few reasons. The first one is that when you build a system and people actually use it, you get feedback you simply cannot get any other way. You learn what the real problems are, not the problems you imagined sitting in your office. Many of the most interesting research questions I've worked on came from users telling us, "This doesn't work for my workload," or "This is too slow," or "I need to do this thing you never thought about." That feedback loop is incredibly valuable for shaping the research agenda.

The second reason is impact. At the end of the day, as researchers, we want our ideas to matter. You can write a paper and it gets cited, and that's good, but if you build something like Spark or Ray and millions of people use it, your ideas get into the world in a very direct way. You're changing how people actually compute. I think that's one of the highest forms of impact an academic can have.

And the third thing, which people underestimate, is that building real systems is extremely hard, and that difficulty is where the research is. It's easy to build a prototype that works on a benchmark. It's much harder to build something that works across a thousand different use cases, that's robust, that scales, that handles failures. When you try to do that, you discover the fundamental problems. The abstractions you thought were right turn out to be wrong, and you have to rethink them. So building usable systems isn't a distraction from research. In my experience, it's the best way to find the research problems worth solving.

Of course, it's also a great way to train students. The students who have built these systems with us, they come out knowing how to go from an idea to something real, and that's a skill that serves them whether they stay in academia or go to industry or start companies.

astra-6.text:
For me, building a system that people actually use is a way to test your research ideas against reality. In a paper, you choose the problem, you make some assumptions, and you evaluate your solution. But when somebody else uses the system, they bring requirements and workloads you may never have considered. You find out which assumptions hold and which ones don’t.

And that feedback creates new research questions. Why is this hard to deploy? Why does performance fall apart for this workload? Can we make the system simpler without losing its capabilities? These can be fundamental problems, but you discover them because people are trying to do something real.

So I see a very productive cycle: research ideas lead to systems, people use those systems, and their experience leads to better research questions. Adoption isn’t the only measure of good research, of course, but it is a powerful way to learn whether you are solving a problem that matters.

r001.rationale: It says real users surface overlooked requirements and generate research questions, but does not explain that building in a new area gives researchers a privileged position to discover that area’s emerging problems.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that problems industry has left unsolved may not be important at the present time.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, building a system that people actually use is a way of testing whether your research assumptions are right. When you write a paper, you choose the problem and the setting in which you evaluate your solution. Real users bring workloads and requirements that you didn’t anticipate. They expose what you missed, and often those surprises lead to new research questions.

There’s also something very satisfying about taking an idea beyond a paper and seeing it help somebody do something they couldn’t do before. That doesn’t mean every research project needs to become a product. But getting a system used gives you a feedback loop: you develop ideas, see where they work and where they break, and use that experience to do better research.
